card: Religion: whose smiling face is on Ash's coin?
messages:
James leans a little closer before the stone settles, and he catches it: not silver, not tarnish — old gold gone black in the river, with the salt eating the lie off it at the edges. The face on it smiles at him out of the dark, and for a beat his mind turns over the old coiners' names and the faces of the southern gods, the minted saints, the queens of Tethyr with their hair in coins.

[Roll card] James Worgen · Skill check — Religion: whose smiling face is on Ash's coin?
What adds to the die: +2 Religion +3 (warlock)
DC 15
The die is cast on the server; tap it to see how it fell.

[Roll the die]

The coin's face comes clear all at once, the way a word does when you stop trying to remember it. What the river-black could not hide: the high, thin brows, the smile that is not bland, that shows no teeth and no kindness, bent round a face cut for a coin three times older than Tethyr and minted to be put into the hands of the dead. The face of Beshaba, Tymora's dark sister, who pours bad luck out of a horn.

No, not Beshaba. The woman on the coin is not the Lady Smiling with mischief, nor the Maid of Misfortune with her wild hair. The line of the jaw is too clean, the smile too knowing. It's the face men in the south press into wax to carry in a pouch, the old salt-goddess exactly as she was before the temples agreed to stop putting her face on money: Umberlee.

Which is worse.

The stone settles onto the jar, and the little room is very quiet again. The cat pads back from the door and sits down beside the stool, not looking at the shelf anymore. Mirri is watching James's face, because Hesper has closed her eyes, the way you do when a thing is finally said in front of a witness.

When Hesper opens her eyes, she doesn't ask James what he saw. She knows by his face that he knows.

"Not by her will." Her voice has gone rough at the edges. "They come up in the harbour with a coin in the mouth. Been two of them my daughter knew. A year back, before you came. The Fist said both of them were drunk and fell in, and the tide did the rest." She looks at the salt jar. "But they don't keep the coins. Whoever puts them there takes it back out and into the blood. That's the old way to pay the sea, not to bury a man."

She does something then with her hands on the table, not reading, not asking — just folding her shawl back over her wrists, one over the other, the way women do before they carry bad news a long way.

"If Ash went under," she says, "he went under to give it back. Or he went under after somebody who took it." Her yellow eyes find James's. "And that's the last thing I know. You've heard it all, soldier. I can't read the river. The cards don't go down there."

Place: Hesper's house · Time: Day 1 · evening

The stone is back on the jar, but the face stays behind your eyes as you turn from the hearth: the river-gold with the salt-rime burning at its edge, and under it the woman smiling up out of the black. It is not Beshaba, though for one beat the shadowed brow could have been hers. It is not Umberlee, though old sailors and old coiners have argued that for centuries, whether the Bitch Queen and the Lord of Murder ever shared a face at the bottom of the sea. You know better, because a warlock of Lady Luck learns the difference between a dark sister and a death-god the way a soldier learns the difference between a bad frost and the plague.

The face on the coin is Bhaal.

Hesper sees it land. Her hand goes still on the edge of the Broken Tower card, and the fire pops behind her as if the room itself had been holding its breath.

"You know it, then." Her voice is lower than it was, and not all the way steady. "You can say it. The cards won't hear any better than they have."

Mirri has gone very still by the hearth, one hand inside her too-big coat, her eyes moving between the old woman and the stranger. She doesn't know the face. But she knows to be afraid when Gran asks a soldier to put a name to gold.

The cat has returned to the leg of the stool. *Say it,* he says, soft. *Then watch the salt.* He doesn't mean the jar. He means the whole house, the night around it, the close wet air that comes off the Chionthar at dusk like a smell from under the world.

· Change: Ash's coin (The face is Bhaal's, not Umberlee's; the player rolled a 25. This is now settled in the campaign: it is a coin of Bhaal, an old murder-tithe from under the city.)
